title: Daring to Be Dull
author: Ashley Murphy
summary: Ashley Murphy, who works with Molly Graham's leadership team, shares the one idea she took from interviewing Matt Abrahams, author of Think Faster, Talk Smarter. The paradox is that giving yourself permission to be mediocre makes you a better and more compelling speaker. When people aim for perfection they lean on mental shortcuts called heuristics, which pull them out of the present moment. Murphy used the idea in a toast at her best friend's wedding, where staying present let her read the room and actually enjoy the occasion. She explains that the improv-derived invitation to dare to be dull means choosing the obvious, which turns out to be the fastest route to being original and genuine. The same habit helps at work, where she now offers ideas grounded in what she actually thinks instead of hunting for the one idea that transforms the conversation.
points: Murphy's central claim is that permission to be mediocre makes a speaker more compelling, because perfectionism pushes people into heuristics and out of the present moment.
Being present while speaking lets you notice confusion or distraction in the audience and adjust in real time, which is the practical payoff for a leader.
Dare to be dull is an improv principle: state the obvious, because the obvious is the quickest path to something original and genuine.
Her wedding toast improved once she stopped engineering an Oscar-worthy speech and simply said what was true about her friend.
At work she now contributes ideas grounded in what she actually thinks, rather than straining to deliver the one idea that transforms the conversation.
quotes: the more permission you give yourself to be mediocre, the better and more compelling a speaker you become.
when we shoot for perfection, we lean on mental shortcuts called heuristics. They’re helpful in plenty of ways, but they have one big flaw. They pull us out of the present moment.
But being present when you speak at work unlocks quite a bit, too. You can see when people get confused or distracted, and adjust.
The idea is that choosing to be obvious is, surprisingly, the fastest path to being original and genuine.
I needed to state the obvious: I love my friend. I love his fiancé. I was thrilled about their wedding, and I couldn’t imagine a better match.
Accepting the dare let me write something much better than whatever my perfectionist self would have come up with.

Instead of feeling pressure to contribute THE idea that transforms the conversation, I’ve been trying to share ideas that are grounded in what I actually think and useful for moving the conversation forward.
